newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says EMU basis for political union.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says EMU basis for political union.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Sunday the single European currency was an important step toward political union in Europe, and the best way to ensure peace and freedom in the coming century.
But a dissonant chorus of other commentators showed the issue was far from settled in Germany.
While Finance Minister Theo Waigel said earlier in the weekend EMU was inconceivable without France, critics said France should only get a ticket if it makes the grade.

Some said the euro, due to start in January 1999, should be delayed, others that that would end the project forever, and some said it was time to end the pointless argument and get down to the business of preparing for the single currency.
"The construction of the House of Europe is the best preparation for peace and freedom in the 21st century," Kohl told a Protestant gathering.
Earlier, Kohl said Germany would do everything it could to meet the criteria for European monetary union (EMU), and that delay would endanger the integration process in Europe.

"We have to take advantage of the historical chance we have with the introduction of the euro," Kohl said. "The federal government will do everything it can to fulfil the stability criteria as outlined in the Maastricht Treaty."

Waigel said EMU would be inconceivable without France's participation, despite recent statements from Paris that this year's budget deficit was likely to exceed the Maastricht Treaty limit of three percent of GDP.
Asked by journalists if EMU were conceivable without France, Waigel said: "Only theoretically, not practically."
Waigel also said Germany will reach the three percent of GDP target despite the new estimate that its federal deficit would rise to 70 billion marks.
"We will make it," Waigel said.

But the finance minister of Waigel's conservative home state of Bavaria kept up the Christian Social Union's (CSU) sniping attacks for a strict interpretation of the treaty, saying EMU could well start without France if that country does not meet the entry criteria.

"If France fails to meet the 3.0 percent criterion this year, Paris cannot belong to the circle of participants until it meets the criterion," Erwin Huber told the news magazine Focus. "It is thoroughly conceivable that EMU will start without France."

Huber was responding to comments by French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn that France's deficit will be above three percent of GDP this year, which is the key year for deciding the starting EMU participants.
Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a hardline advocate of a strict interpretation of the EMU rules, recently won a pledge from Kohl that the 3.0 percent rule should be strictly applied.

The eurosceptic side was joined by at least one prominent member of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD). Heinz Schleusser, finance minister of North Rhine-Westphalia, said EMU should be delayed if Germay does not meet the convergence criteria.

"The stability of the euro is more important than the schedule for introducing it. The citizens must have trust in the new European currency," Schleusser said in an interview with Bild am Sonntag newspaper.
His remarks echoed recent comments by German eurosceptics from opposite political camps: Gerhard Schroeder, SPD premier of Lower Saxony, and Stoiber, premier of Bavaria.

But others in the leftist camp warned the German government not to gamble away union and other support for the European single currency by implementing further social spending cuts to meet euro entry criteria.

Ursula Engelen-Kefer, vice chairman of the Federation of German trade unions (DGB), said "I warn the government: further cuts in social spending for the euro will be the stumbling block, the breaking point the government won't be able to get past."
"It will gamble away the support of the DGB and the Social Democrats for the euro," she said in an interview with the Cologne daily Express.
Bernhard Vogel, CDU premier of the east German state of Thuringia said German political leaders should end the pointless debate over the introduction of the euro.
"We should put the discussion to rest and make sure that the citizens and the economy get ready," said Vogel in an interview with the Leipziger Zeitung newspaper.
